Thursday at the Walgreens drive-thru I had a very good morning. I gave the pharmacist my prescription number from memory, all nine digits, and she actually said wow. Then I parked to run inside for cough drops, swung both legs out like a woman on a mission, and got yanked right back into the seat like a dog on a leash. Twice. The second time I really committed. A teenager in a hoodie watched the whole thing from the cart return and politely looked away. Nine digits, though. Nobody can take that from me.
column6: My husband once watched me try to get out of the car three times before he leaned over and unbuckled me without a word. He didn't have to say anything. That silence has followed me around for eleven years now. He still brings it up at Thanksgiving.

column2: The electric bill came on Tuesday and I opened it standing up, which was my first mistake. I sat down for the second page. Then I went to the store for eggs, bread, and the store-brand coffee, and the girl at the register said forty-one dollars like it was perfectly normal. My friend Linda keeps sending me pictures from her cruise. Turquoise water, little towel animals folded on the bed. Good for Linda. I don't want the cruise. I want eggs to stop acting like a luxury good. Linda can keep the towel swan.
column6: I keep a running list on the fridge of what things used to cost. Stamps, gas, a movie ticket, a gallon of milk. My grandkids think it's a history project. It's not a history project. It's a grievance with a magnet on it.

column2: There's a photo of my mother hanging laundry in 1974, and I look at it more than I'd like to admit. Four kids, one car, a clothesline that ran from the porch to the maple tree. We had hand-me-downs, and they were pressed. We had casserole on Wednesdays, and we said please and thank you or we didn't get the casserole. Nobody called it a budget. It was just how the week went. I didn't know until I was grown how hard she worked to make it look easy. I still thank the waitress twice.
column6: My dad wore the same brown cardigan every Sunday for about fifteen years, and the elbows were patched twice. When I cleaned out his closet I found it folded in tissue paper. He never had much. He took care of every bit of it. I kept the cardigan.

column2: At 2:14 this morning I was under the quilt, the fleece, and the weighted one my sister gave me for Christmas. At 2:31 I had kicked all three onto the floor and was lying there with one foot hanging off the bed like a tired dog. By 3:00 I wanted the fleece back. My husband has moved to the guest room until further notice, and the room seems happier for it. The thermostat is set to 66 and it is not up for discussion. The blankets have their own nightstand now. Everyone in this house knows their job.
column6: I bought a little clip-on fan for the headboard last month. Best twenty-two dollars I've spent this year. It has three speeds and I use all of them in a single night. My husband calls it the jet engine. He says that from down the hall.

column2: It was the Target parking lot, 6:40 on a Tuesday, already getting dark. I had my keys, my receipt, a bag with two candles I did not need, and no phone. So I checked the cup holder. Under the seat. In the door pocket, where I found a granola bar from what I believe was spring. I was on my knees in the back seat, light shining into every corner, getting worried. Then I went to call it. With it. That was the moment. I sat back there for a minute after that, letting it sink in.
column6: Last week I also spent ten minutes looking for my sunglasses while wearing them. I only figured it out because the sun went behind a cloud and everything got very dark. I've stopped telling my daughter these stories. She's started keeping a list.

column2: Took an online quiz that says I'm a 'free spirit.' It took me 40 minutes to pick a soup at Kroger yesterday.
column6: My daughter sent me the quiz. Twelve questions about beaches and road trips, and apparently I answered like a woman who follows the wind. Then Saturday I stood in the soup aisle holding a chicken noodle and a chicken and stars, reading the labels like a contract. I went with neither. I bought crackers.

column2: Everyone talks about the hot flashes. Nobody mentions that somewhere around 51 my ears got an upgrade nobody asked for. Sunday dinner, my brother-in-law Gary was eating a salad across the table and I could hear every single crouton. Every one. Then he started on the celery. I put my fork down and looked at him. He asked if something was wrong and I said Gary, I can hear your teeth thinking. My sister laughed so hard she had to leave the room. Gary finished his plate in the kitchen. I didn't ask him to. He just knew.
column6: My husband eats cereal at 10 at night standing at the counter, and I can hear it from the bedroom with the door closed and the TV on. I've asked him to switch to oatmeal. He says that's not the same experience. Neither is mine.

column2: Saturday afternoon I had the windows down and the radio up, singing Heart like I had a stadium waiting on me. Sunglasses on, hair doing exactly what I asked it to, one hand out the window riding the wind. I was magnificent. Then I hit the roundabout by the new Costco. Somebody honked, a sign said something about a detour, and before I even thought about it my hand reached over and turned the volume all the way down. Like the music was blocking my eyes. I leaned toward the windshield and squinted. Barracuda went quietly. She understood.
column6: My mother used to do the exact same thing and I used to roll my eyes from the back seat. I'd like to formally apologize to her, about thirty years late. She was right. You cannot merge and listen to Fleetwood Mac at the same time. Nobody can.

column2: At 7:15 this morning I was wearing a fleece robe and wool socks and still couldn't feel my fingers. By 7:40 I had the freezer door open and my face very close to the frozen peas. I've started dressing in layers like I'm climbing Everest, peeling things off and putting them back on so often that my coworker asked if I was okay. I said I'm fine, I'm just weather now. There's a cardigan on the back of every chair in this house. The dog steps over the discarded socks. We've all adjusted. Mostly me.
column6: I keep a little battery fan in my purse, another in the car, and one at my desk at work. Last week I lost all three on the same day. Found one in the freezer. I have no memory of putting it there, but I understand why I did.

column2: My cat Pickles has never once worried about anything. Last night I watched him look me dead in the eye and push my reading glasses off the nightstand, one slow paw at a time. Then he walked away like a man who'd just closed a business deal. Meanwhile I had spent the whole afternoon on hold with the insurance company over a $38 charge. Two transfers. One dropped call. A man named Kevin who asked me to spell my name three times. Pickles has the right idea. Some things don't need a phone call. They need a table edge and some nerve.
column6: Today I left a voicemail for the HOA about the mailbox thing, and I hung up mid-sentence when I decided I'd said enough. I didn't even say goodbye. I just walked into the kitchen. Pickles was sitting on the counter watching me. I think he was proud.

column2: My cousin's retirement party was at the Elks lodge on Saturday, and I was forty minutes late because of a zipper situation I won't go into. By the time I got there everyone was already seated. So I did what any reasonable woman would do. I paused in the doorway, adjusted one earring, and took a long look around the room like I was deciding whether it deserved me. Three people stopped talking. My aunt Rita set her fork down. Nobody needed to know about the zipper. As far as that room knows, I arrived exactly when I meant to.
column6: My sister says I've walked into rooms this way since the third grade, when I showed up to picture day wearing one shoe. I don't remember the shoe. I remember the photographer saying whatever you're doing, keep doing it. I haven't stopped since.

column2: The new washer came with an app. I didn't know a washer needed an app, but there it was, asking me to create a password before it would tell me the jeans were done. My mother's machine lived in the basement for twenty-six years. It had one knob and it sounded like a small airplane, and in all that time it never once needed Wi-Fi. Last Thursday mine needed an update in the middle of a cycle. The towels just sat there in the water, waiting with me. I've ordered a clothesline. Nobody's going to update that.
column6: The repairman came out on Monday, looked at the screen for a while, then turned it off and back on. That was the whole visit. It was ninety-five dollars. I've started turning myself off and on when things get complicated. Works about as well.
